correctness.rationale: Reconstructed from the strict-positive constant-value premise: individual inter-EF1 iff count spread <=1. Under item-based realized center valuations, counterfactual reassignment after deleting a rival good gives the two exact inequalities \(a+b\ge c+d-1\) and \(c+\varepsilon d\ge a+b-1\). For \(m=4q+r\), \(q\ge1\), these force the four explicit canonical patterns; every excluded alternative demands \(\varepsilon\ge1\) or violates center-one EF1. Direct substitution yields the exact inclusive four-residue threshold, and each canonical pattern constructs a feasible allocation. The independent exact-rational enumerator verified 1,122 inventory/discount instances for \(4\le m\le80\) and explicit small-boundary cases. The code is finite corroboration only; the all-m proof is symbolic and self-contained.

originality.rationale: The same-object source arXiv:2607.27743, Theorem 11, gives the twelve-good nonexistence witness for three unit agents and one uniformly discounted agent under item-based realized centers. It does not determine the exact feasibility threshold at every inventory size or the eight/nine/ten reversal. The stronger-looking balanced EF1 existence theorems arXiv:2603.05956 and arXiv:2608.06325 concern only individual-agent fairness and cannot enforce delegated center EF1; their statements neither subsume nor refute this classification. Targeted public-literature and mathematical-results searches yielded no decisive equivalent. This is best-knowledge originality, not proof of publication priority.

value.rationale: The naturally motivated published one-discounted-agent obstruction had a twelve-good example with an unspecified small discount. This claim resolves the precise full-inventory robustness frontier for the same four-agent model, establishes the first obstruction within that family at \(m=8\), and shows the nontrivial nonmonotone eight/nine/ten sequence as goods are added. It explains the tradeoff between individual count balance and center realized-versus-counterfactual welfare, an issue not captured by ordinary balanced EF1. It neither relies on an arbitrary artificial slice nor asserts general-minimum or broader efficiency theorems.
